issues.location: "Classless addressing replaced three fixed sizes" section, the sentence "RFC 4632 spells out why that stopped working: no size in between, so 'an organization that needed slightly more than 254 host addresses would ... require a Class B address' thousands of times bigger than needed"
issues.problem: This is presented in quotation marks as a verbatim citation of RFC 4632 section 2, but no such sentence exists in that RFC. I independently fetched RFC 4632 section 2 and confirmed the actual text is: "Class C, with a maximum of 254 host addresses, is too small, whereas Class B, which allows up to 65534 host addresses, is too large for most organizations." A Google policy reviewer treats a fabricated quotation dressed up with an ellipsis and attributed to a real, checkable standards document as exactly the kind of trust violation E-E-A-T guidelines exist to catch — it is worse than an unsupported claim because it actively misrepresents a source the article cites elsewhere accurately (RFC 791, RFC 1918, RFC 3021, RFC 3022, RFC 4291, RFC 5737, RFC 3849 and the IPNetwork/bitwise-operators Microsoft Learn pages all check out verbatim). One fabricated citation sitting next to eight accurate ones is the specific failure mode that makes a site's sourcing look unreliable on inspection, not just occasionally imprecise. This alone is enough to withhold a pass regardless of how strong the rest of the article is.
issues.fixLooksLike: Replace the quoted fragment with RFC 4632's real wording ("Class C, with a maximum of 254 host addresses, is too small, whereas Class B, ... is too large for most organizations") or paraphrase the same point in the writer's own words with the quotation marks removed, keeping the citation link to RFC 4632 section 2.

issues.location: "What System.Net.IPNetwork does when the bits don't line up" section, the sentence "Both `TryParse` and the plain `Parse` accepted the misaligned pair and quietly normalized it to `203.0.113.64/26`"
issues.problem: The article's own run block (id=ipnetwork-quirk) only calls `IPNetwork.TryParse`; the plain `Parse` overload is never invoked or shown in the article. I ran it myself on this machine (.NET 10.0.401) and confirmed `IPNetwork.Parse("203.0.113.81/26")` does in fact also return `203.0.113.64/26` without throwing, so the claim happens to be true — but the article states it as a tested fact ("Tested on .NET 10.0.401 ... it does not throw") while only showing evidence for half of that claim. Per the brief's rule that a factual claim be "proved by a run block in the article," a reader (or a future edit) has no way to verify the `Parse` half from the article's own visible code.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add a second call in the same run block, e.g. `IPNetwork net2 = IPNetwork.Parse(cidr); Console.WriteLine($"Parse   {net2}");`, and show its output line, so both claimed behaviors are actually demonstrated rather than one being asserted by extension.

justification: node tools/check-article.mjs networking/ip-addresses-and-subnets: PASS (words=4495 prose=2742 run=12 fig=2 sources=10 flesch=54.9, 0 errors/0 warnings). node tools/run-code.mjs: PASS (blocks=24 executed=12, every shown output matches a real run). Playing an adversarial Google policy reviewer hunting for low-value content, I compared this article against the current top results for 'subnetting explained' / 'what is CIDR': I fetched and read AWS's 'What is CIDR?' (introductory prose, no bit-level mask derivation, no VLSM, no runnable code, no RFC 1918 coverage, no private-range or NAT discussion) and PracticalNetworking.net's subnetting series (practitioner/exam-oriented video course, no VLSM, no IPv6, no private ranges, no primary-source citations in its visible content). This article is substantively deeper and more original than both: it derives every claim from bit arithmetic shown running in C#, checks its own hand-rolled math against .NET's own IPNetwork type, and surfaces a genuine, non-obvious, verifiably real gap between IPNetwork's documented 'will throw' contract and its actual non-throwing behavior on .NET 10.0.401 — something none of the compared pages, and no other source I found via web search, mentions. I searched for five of the article's distinctive non-quoted sentences (the opening scenario, the mask-AND explanation, the /12-boundary framing, the IPv6 trade-off framing, the 'do not build validation on undocumented exception behavior' advice) and found no matching or near-matching passages anywhere on the web; the worked VLSM scenario (100/50/20-host tiers packed into 203.0.113.0/24) is a generic problem shape but the specific numbers, addresses and code are original. Structurally the article is not templated: its eight h2 headings ('Thirty-two bits, written as four decimal numbers', 'The prefix length says how many bits are fixed', etc.) are specific to its own content and share no boilerplate with sibling articles how-the-internet-works.md, tcp-vs-udp.md, dns.md and http-explained.md, which each use their own distinct heading sets; there is no 'Introduction'/'Conclusion'/'Key Takeaways' section; the opening paragraph delivers a concrete scenario instead of throat-clearing; and the four exercises are genuinely varied in form (hand-compute-then-verify, find-the-bug, extend-the-code, membership test) rather than reusing 'predict the output' every time, satisfying the pilot-round lesson on varying the ending. I grepped the article for mass-produced-text tells ('in other words', 'simply put', 'it's not X, it's Y', 'in today's', 'in conclusion') and found none; paragraph lengths vary organically with the technical content rather than sitting at a uniform length. Cross-links are handled correctly: docs/crosslinks/networking/ip-addresses-and-subnets.md sensibly explains why no links to unpublished siblings are needed (its three prerequisites are already published) and records the boundary with how-the-internet-works.md and tcp-vs-udp.md to avoid duplicate coverage of NAT/ports, which checks out against those articles' own content. Against that strong baseline, however, I independently fetched RFC 4632 section 2 and confirmed the article attributes a fabricated verbatim quotation to it (see the blocker issue) — a real sentence dressed in quotation marks and an ellipsis that does not exist in the source, sitting inside an article whose entire pitch to a policy reviewer is 'every claim is either run or cited to a primary source I actually read.' That is precisely the kind of misrepresented sourcing that costs a site its standing on trustworthiness, and it is not a nit: it must be fixed regardless of how strong everything else is. I also flag a second, much smaller instance of the same pattern (a claim about `IPNetwork.Parse` that I verified is true, but that the article's own code does not demonstrate). Neither issue reflects filler, duplication, keyword stuffing or thin content — the opposite failure mode, in fact, an unusually deep and original article let down by one bad citation — but the fabrication caps the score well below 'ships with nits' until it is corrected.
